blocks.text: A cast bracket with a curved fillet is meshed automatically with thousands of tiny triangles, while a straight machined beam next to it is meshed by hand with a few large quadrilaterals. Both choices are defensible. The shape functions of the element, not the number of nodes alone, decide how well it follows a bending stress field, and that is what you must learn to judge.

blocks.markdown: **Why element order matters.** Within an element the displacement is a polynomial built from the shape functions, and strain is its derivative. A **linear** element (three-node triangle or four-node quadrilateral) has a strain field that is constant or only partly linear. A **quadratic** element has a strain field that contains a complete linear variation: for the six-node triangle the strain varies linearly, and for the eight-node (serendipity) quadrilateral it varies quadratically in general (a complete linear part plus some quadratic terms). In a bending-dominated member the axial strain varies linearly through the depth, so linear elements have to approximate it with steps.

blocks.title: Order of convergence
blocks.text: For smooth solutions with polynomial order $p$ the displacement error falls like $h^{p+1}$ and the stress (strain) error like $h^{p}$, where $h$ is the element size (m). Halving $h$ cuts the displacement error by a factor $2^{p+1}$: 4 for linear and 8 for quadratic elements. These rates are asymptotic and assume the solution is smooth.

blocks.markdown: **Area coordinates.** For a triangle with nodes $(x_i,y_i)$, $i=1,2,3$ numbered counter-clockwise, the shape functions are the **area coordinates** $L_i$: $L_i$ is the ratio of the area of the sub-triangle formed by the point and the side opposite node $i$ to the total area $A$ (m$^2$). They satisfy $L_i=1$ at node $i$, $L_i=0$ on the opposite side and $L_1+L_2+L_3=1$. For the linear triangle $N_i=L_i$.

blocks.title: Area coordinates at an interior point
blocks.prompt: A linear triangle has nodes (in mm) 1: (1,1), 2: (7,2), 3: (3,5). Find its area and the shape functions at the point $(3,\,2.5)$.

steps.text: Area: $2A=(x_2-x_1)(y_3-y_1)-(x_3-x_1)(y_2-y_1)=(6)(4)-(2)(1)=22$, so $A=11$ mm$^2$ (positive, so the numbering is counter-clockwise).
Check: $L_1+L_2+L_3=1$ and $\sum L_ix_i=3$, $\sum L_iy_i=2.5$, so the point is reproduced exactly and lies inside because all three values are positive.

blocks.caption: Choosing an element family

blocks.title: Constant strain in a linear triangle
blocks.prompt: A linear triangle has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (5,0), 3: (1,4). Nodal displacements (mm): $u=(0,\,0.010,\,0.004)$ and $v=(0,\,0,\,0.002)$. Find $\varepsilon_x$, $\varepsilon_y$ and $\gamma_{xy}$.

steps.text: Since $u=\sum L_iu_i$ and $L_{i,x}=b_i/2A$, we get $\varepsilon_x=\sum b_iu_i/(2A)=(4)(0.010)/20=0.002$.
None of these depend on position, so the strain is uniform over the whole triangle. A linear bending strain through the depth can therefore only be approximated by a step for each layer of triangles.

blocks.answer: Strains are uniform over the element: $\varepsilon_x=2.0\times10^{-3}$, $\varepsilon_y=5.0\times10^{-4}$, $\gamma_{xy}=5.0\times10^{-4}$ (dimensionless).

items: Identify the dominant behaviour (bending, membrane or local stress concentration).
If the strain varies strongly through a thickness, use quadratic elements or several linear elements through the depth.
Use triangles or tetrahedra where geometry is too complex to map into quadrilaterals or bricks, preferably quadratic.
Use mapped quadrilateral meshes in regular regions and check convergence by refinement.

blocks.title: Triangles are not automatically bad
blocks.text: The constant-strain triangle is stiff and needs a fine mesh, but the quadratic triangle is accurate and is the standard choice for automatically meshed curved parts. Do not mix element orders across a shared edge without compatible nodes or constraints.

points: Linear elements have constant or incomplete linear strain; quadratic elements contain a complete linear strain variation, so they represent a linearly varying strain such as bending exactly (the six-node triangle varies linearly, the eight-node quadrilateral quadratically in general).
Displacement error scales as $h^{p+1}$ and stress error as $h^{p}$ for smooth problems.
The linear triangle has shape functions equal to area coordinates, $L_i=(a_i+b_ix+c_iy)/(2A)$, summing to 1.
Use triangles for free meshing of complex shapes and quadrilaterals for regular, bending-dominated regions, with quadratic order preferred when accuracy matters.

questions.stem: In a linear triangle with area coordinates $L_1,L_2,L_3$, what is the value of $L_1$ at the centroid of the triangle?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the centroid is equidistant from all three sides, so each area coordinate equals one third.
distractorRationale.b: This is the value at the midpoint of an edge adjacent to node 1, not at the centroid.
distractorRationale.c: $L_1=0$ holds along the side opposite node 1 only.

questions.explanation: The three sub-triangles formed with the centroid have equal areas, each one third of the total. Hence $L_1=L_2=L_3=1/3$, and the sum is 1 as required.

questions.stem: A linear triangle has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (6,0), 3: (2,4), numbered counter-clockwise. Find the value of the shape function $N_2=L_2$ at the point $(3,\,1)$ (dimensionless).

A linear triangle has nodes (in mm) 1: (0,0), 2: (4,0), 3: (0,3). The axial displacements of the nodes are $u_1=0$, $u_2=0.004$ mm and $u_3=0.001$ mm. Find the uniform strain $\varepsilon_x$ in microstrain ($10^{-6}$).
questions.explanation: Here $2A=12$ mm$^2$ and $b=(y_2-y_3,\,y_3-y_1,\,y_1-y_2)=(-3,\,3,\,0)$. Then $\varepsilon_x=\sum b_iu_i/(2A)=(3)(0.004)/12=1.0\times10^{-3}$, which is 1000 microstrain. The value is the same at every point of the element.

questions.stem: Why do linear (Q4 or T3) elements perform poorly in a bending-dominated member compared with quadratic elements of similar size?

options.text: Their strain fields cannot follow the linear variation of bending strain through the depth, so the element is too stiff
Quadratic elements have fewer degrees of freedom
Linear elements cannot represent rigid-body motion
Linear elements always give negative strain energy

questions.correctOptionText: Their strain fields cannot follow the linear variation of bending strain through the depth, so the element is too stiff

distractorRationale.a: Correct: bending strain varies linearly with distance from the neutral axis, which a constant (or incompletely linear) strain field cannot match.
distractorRationale.b: Quadratic elements have more nodes and therefore more degrees of freedom, not fewer.
distractorRationale.c: Linear elements represent rigid-body motion perfectly, which is a basic requirement.
distractorRationale.d: Strain energy is positive for any valid element; the problem is stiffness, not sign.

questions.explanation: The element has to follow a linearly varying strain with constant or partly linear strain, so it either steps or develops spurious shear, and the model is too stiff. Quadratic elements carry a linearly varying strain and capture bending much better.

questions.stem: A single layer of eight-node quadratic quadrilaterals through the depth of a straight beam can represent pure bending exactly, whereas a single layer of four-node linear quadrilaterals cannot.
questions.explanation: True. The quadratic displacement field contains the terms needed for the linear bending strain variation through depth. The bilinear field produces a spurious shear strain, so one layer of linear elements locks.

questions.stem: A quadratic-element model of a bracket gives a tip displacement error of 2.4% relative to the converged value. Assuming the asymptotic rate $h^{p+1}$ for smooth solutions, what displacement error in percent would you expect after halving the element size everywhere?
questions.explanation: For quadratic elements $p=2$, so the displacement error scales as $h^{3}$. Halving $h$ reduces it by $2^3=8$, giving $2.4/8=0.3\%$. This holds only in the asymptotic range of a smooth problem, not near singularities.

questions.stem: A cast component with curved fillets and varying thickness is to be meshed automatically in two dimensions. Which element choice is most appropriate?

options.text: Quadratic (six-node) triangles, because they follow curved boundaries and fill arbitrary shapes while capturing linear strain
Linear three-node triangles only, because they are cheapest and equally accurate
Single large four-node quadrilaterals with one point integration
Eight-node quadrilaterals only, because triangles are not allowed in two dimensions

questions.correctOptionText: Quadratic (six-node) triangles, because they follow curved boundaries and fill arbitrary shapes while capturing linear strain

distractorRationale.a: Correct: automatic free meshing relies on triangles, and quadratic ones remove the stiffness of the constant-strain triangle.
distractorRationale.b: Linear triangles are not equally accurate; their constant strain requires a much finer mesh.
distractorRationale.c: A few large linear quadrilaterals cannot fit complicated curved geometry or resolve fillet stresses.
distractorRationale.d: Triangles are permitted and standard for free meshing; quadrilateral-only meshing is difficult for complex shapes.

questions.explanation: Triangles fill arbitrary two-dimensional regions automatically, and using quadratic order gives accuracy without needing an extremely fine mesh. This is why six-node triangles or ten-node tetrahedra are the usual choice for complex castings.

questions.stem: A long, thin, straight cantilever strip loaded in bending is to be modelled with a mapped mesh. Which choice gives the most accurate result for a coarse mesh?

options.text: Quadratic quadrilaterals with at least one layer through the depth, with elements stretched along the length
Linear three-node triangles with one layer through the depth
Linear four-node quadrilaterals with one layer through the depth and full integration
Mixed random orientation of linear triangles

questions.correctOptionText: Quadratic quadrilaterals with at least one layer through the depth, with elements stretched along the length

distractorRationale.a: Correct: regular geometry suits mapped quadrilaterals, and the quadratic field represents bending strain.
distractorRationale.b: One layer of constant-strain triangles badly underestimates bending deflection.
distractorRationale.c: One layer of bilinear elements with full integration locks in bending.
distractorRationale.d: Random orientation adds mesh-direction bias without improving the strain field.

questions.explanation: Geometry is regular, so a mapped quadrilateral mesh is feasible, and quadratic order supplies the linearly varying strain needed for bending. This beats linear triangles or locked linear quadrilaterals on the same mesh.

questions.stem: A colleague models a slender cantilever loaded at its tip with one layer of four-node quadrilaterals and finds the tip deflection is 70% of the beam-theory value. Explain the likely cause and give two ways of improving the model, justifying your choice of element type.
markingGuide: Cause: bilinear element cannot bend without a spurious shear strain, so shear locking makes it too stiff
Slender members make the effect worse, since the shear energy dominates
Fix 1: use quadratic (eight-node) elements, which represent the linear bending strain
Fix 2: use several linear elements through the depth, or reduced integration/incompatible modes, with a convergence check
Compare the refined result with the beam-theory value to verify
questions.explanation: A coarse mesh of linear elements overestimates stiffness in bending because the element cannot follow the linear strain gradient. Raising element order or refining through the depth reduces the error.

questions.stem: Derive the three area coordinates of a linear triangle in terms of position, and show that they have the properties needed of shape functions: unit value at their own node, zero on the opposite side, and sum equal to one. Why does this make the element able to represent a uniform strain?
markingGuide: Area coordinate $L_i=$ area of sub-triangle opposite node $i$ divided by $A$, giving $L_i=(a_i+b_ix+c_iy)/2A$
At node $i$ the sub-triangle becomes the whole triangle so $L_i=1$; on the opposite side its area is zero so $L_i=0$
Sum of the three sub-triangle areas equals $A$, so $\sum L_i=1$
Positions are reproduced: $x=\sum L_ix_i$, $y=\sum L_iy_i$, so the field is a complete linear polynomial
A linear displacement field gives constant derivatives, hence a uniform strain is represented exactly
questions.explanation: Area coordinates are geometric ratios, so their nodal and sum properties follow directly. Because they span a complete linear polynomial the element can reproduce rigid motion and uniform strain.
